topic_and_scope: A structured analysis of emerging diagnostic imaging technologies in dentistry (2019–2024) with emphasis on AI, CBCT, MAPs, biosensors, and biomaterials, focusing on how these innovations reshape diagnosis, planning, and minimally invasive interventions. The work also considers methodological approaches, adoption challenges, and calls for future research to advance clinical validation, standardization, and accessibility.
main_themes: Advances in imaging modalities and AI-driven diagnostics (CBCT, AI analysis, 3D printing/MAPs, intraoral ultrasonography with AI)
Molecular and biomaterial integration with imaging for personalized dental care (biomarkers, biosensors, biomaterials in planning and rehabilitation)
Implementation challenges, ethics, economics, and policy including validation, standardization, accessibility, and regulatory considerations
main_findings: Emerging imaging technologies, including CBCT, AI-based image analysis, 3D printing-enabled MAPs, and biosensors, are driving higher diagnostic accuracy and enabling personalized, minimally invasive treatment planning in dentistry.

Despite these advances, adoption is constrained by high costs, need for specialized training, data privacy and algorithmic bias concerns, and a lack of broad clinical validation and standardized AI-driven diagnostic frameworks.

key_gaps.description: Explicit gaps include the clinical validation of emerging diagnostic technologies, accessibility issues across resource settings, and the need for standardization in AI-driven dental diagnostics.

Implied gaps involve geographic and resource-based disparities in research and adoption, limited longitudinal data and small study sizes in the current literature, and the absence of comprehensive, multi-database bibliometric coverage to map global trends fully.

future_directions.title: Large-scale clinical validation of AI-assisted CBCT and ultrasound diagnostics across diverse populations
future_directions.rationale: To determine real-world diagnostic accuracy, safety, and impact on patient outcomes, it is essential to conduct multicenter, prospective trials and, where feasible, randomized studies comparing AI-assisted imaging to standard care. These studies should include diverse patient demographics, varying disease severities, and different practice settings (academic, private, and low-resource clinics). Data collected should cover diagnostic performance, treatment planning changes, procedural outcomes, and patient satisfaction, enabling robust generalization and regulatory support.

future_directions.title: Develop and implement standardized AI governance and benchmarking in dentistry
future_directions.rationale: Create consensus-driven standards for data quality, model transparency, bias mitigation, and reporting in dental AI research. Establish open, diverse benchmarking datasets and clear evaluation metrics to allow fair comparisons across algorithms and imaging modalities. Publishing with standardized reporting will facilitate regulatory review, clinical translation, and reproducibility across institutions.

future_directions.title: Comprehensive cost-effectiveness and implementation research for CBCT, AI, and MAPs
future_directions.rationale: Assess the economic value and practical feasibility of adopting advanced imaging technologies in a range of settings, including small practices and underserved regions. Studies should compare total costs, workflow impact, learning curves, and long-term patient outcomes, providing decision-makers with evidence to guide investments, reimbursement strategies, and scalable deployment models.

future_directions.title: Creation of integrated clinical workflows and digital twin approaches for dental care
future_directions.rationale: Develop and pilot standardized workflows that integrate AI analysis, CBCT imaging, MAP-based modeling, and digital prosthodontic planning within existing electronic dental records and practice management systems. Trials should assess improvements in diagnostic precision, surgical planning accuracy, patient communication, and treatment timelines, with training modules for clinicians.

future_directions.title: Regulatory frameworks and ethical guidelines for dental AI and imaging technologies
future_directions.rationale: Establish clear regulatory pathways addressing data privacy, consent, cross-border data sharing, algorithmic accountability, and post-market surveillance. Guidelines should emphasize bias mitigation, transparency, and patient safety, providing a roadmap for global adoption that respects local regulatory contexts.

future_directions.title: Development of diverse, longitudinal imaging and biomarker datasets for AI training
future_directions.rationale: Invest in multi-institutional data collection efforts that include longitudinal imaging, biomarker profiles, and outcome data from diverse populations. Ensure privacy-preserving data-sharing mechanisms (e.g., de-identification, federated learning) to build robust AI models that generalize across ethnicities, ages, and clinical conditions while minimizing biases.

future_directions.title: Validation of intraoral ultrasonography with AI in periodontics and implantology
future_directions.rationale: Conduct dedicated clinical studies to compare high-frequency intraoral ultrasound with conventional imaging modalities, evaluating diagnostic accuracy for periodontium assessment, implant planning, and early infection detection. Determine patient-centered benefits, such as reduced radiation exposure and improved comfort, to define appropriate use cases.

future_directions.title: Education and workforce development for digital dentistry and AI literacy
future_directions.rationale: Design and evaluate curricula and continuing education programs that equip dentists, hygienists, and technicians with competencies in AI interpretation, CBCT interpretation, MAP/3D printing workflows, and ethical considerations. Include competency assessments and certification pathways to ensure consistent, high-quality clinical practice as technologies evolve.
